topic.name: Calculating Flux in Two-Dimensional Vector Fields

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = (x-16y)\,\mathbf{i} + (x+y)\,\mathbf{j}$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $x^2 + 16y^2 = 16.$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

First, we write the equation of our curve as

\[ \dfrac{x^2}{4^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{1^2} = 1. \]

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $1,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

\[ \mathbf{r}(t) = 4\cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} +\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 4\cos t, \qquad y = \sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= x-16y = 4\cos t - 16 \sin t, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &=x+y = 4\cos t + \sin t. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\cos t) = -4\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sin t) = \cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(4\cos t - 16 \sin t \right) \cdot \big( \cos t \big) - \left(4\cos t + \sin t\right) \cdot \big( -4\sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 4 \cos^2 t - 16 \sin t \cos t + 16 \sin t \cos t + 4 \sin^2 t \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 4 \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= 4t \, \Big|_{0}^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &= 4(2\pi-0) \\[5pt] &= 8\pi \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Cartesian Form

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = y\,\mathbf{i} - 2x\,\mathbf{j}$ across the circle $C$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 = 16.$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

First, we write the equation of our curve as

\[ x^2 + y^2 = 4^2. \]

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $4.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

\[ \mathbf{r}(t) = 4\cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + 4\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 4\cos t, \qquad y = 4\sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= y = 4\sin t, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= -2x =-8\cos t. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\cos t) = -4\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\sin t) = 4\cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\sin t, \textrm d u = \cos t \,\textrm d t,$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left( 4\sin t \right) \cdot \big( 4\cos t \big) - \left(- 8\cos t \right) \cdot \big( -4\sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} (-16\sin t\cos t) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= -16\int_0^{0} u \: \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Cartesian Form

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = 8\,\mathbf{i} - (x+3)\,\mathbf{j}$ across the circle $C$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 = 4.$
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by \[ \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x, \] where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

First, we write the equation of our curve as

\[ x^2 + y^2 = 2^2. \]

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $2.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

\[ \mathbf{r}(t) = 2\cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + 2\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j}, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi. \]

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = 2\cos t, \qquad y = 2\sin t. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= 8, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= x+3 =2\cos t+3. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\cos t) = -2\sin t, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sin t) = 2\cos t. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the double-angle formula for sine, as follows:

\begin{align*} \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \oint\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} \left( 8\right) \cdot \big( 2\cos t \big) - \left(-2\cos t - 3 \right) \cdot \big( -2\sin t \big) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 16\cos t - 4\sin t \cos t - 6\sin t)\: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{2\pi} 16\cos t - 2\sin 2t - 6\sin t)\: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \big(16\sin t - \cos 2t - 6\cos t \big) \, \Bigg|_{0}^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &= 0 \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Cartesian Form

question.text: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) =x\,\mathbf{i} + y^2\,\mathbf{j}$ through the curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = \dfrac{1}{t}\,\mathbf{i} + t \,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in \left[\dfrac{1}{2},2\right],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C$ is given by \[ \int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x. \] To apply this formula,

  • the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

  • the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ must be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$

In this case, $\mathbf n$ is indeed a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf T,$ so we can apply the above formula.

Along the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = \dfrac{1}{t}, \qquad y = t . \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &=x = \dfrac{1}{t}, \\[7pt] Q(x,y) &= y^2 = t^2. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\dfrac 1t\right) = -\dfrac{1}{t^2}, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(t \right) = 1. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \int\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{1/2}^{2} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{1/2}^{2} \left( \dfrac{1}{t} \right) \cdot \left(1 \right) - (t^2) \cdot \left( -\dfrac{1}{t^2} \right) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{1/2}^{2} \dfrac{1}{t} + 1 \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= (\ln t + t )\Bigg|_{1/2}^{2} \\[5pt] &= (\ln 2+ 2) - \left(\ln \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} \right) \\[5pt] &= 2\ln2 + \dfrac{3}{2} \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve

question.text: The curve $C$ is given by $y = x^3$ from the point $\left(0,0\right)$ to the point $\left(1,1\right).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) =-3x^2\,\mathbf{i} + \,\mathbf{j}$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C$ is given by \[ \int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x. \] To apply this formula,

  • the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

  • the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ must be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have \[ x = t, \qquad y = t^3, \qquad t\in \left[0,1\right]. \]

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(1,1).$ Therefore, $\mathbf n$ is indeed a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux.

Therefore,

\begin{align*} P(x,y) &= -3x^2 = -3t^2, \\[5pt] Q(x,y) &= 1. \end{align*}

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t) = 1, \\[10pt] \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(t^3\right) = 3t^2. \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s &= \int\limits_C P \: \text{d}y - Q \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left(P \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} - Q \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \right) \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \left(-3t^2 \right) \cdot \left(3t^2 \right) - \left(1\right) \cdot \left(1\right) \: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} -9t^4-1\: \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \left(-\dfrac{9t^5}{5} - t\right)\Bigg|_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= \left(-\dfrac{9}{5} - 1\right) - 0 \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{14}{5} \end{align*}
